questions: Does InternalServiceTokenFilter match on the raw (encoded) URI or the decoded path, and does Spring MVC's dispatcher route on the same representation?
Is there any global HttpFirewall / UrlPathHelper / path-pattern-matching config that would neutralize a percent-encoded prefix bypass?
Does SecurityConfig have an explicit authorization rule for /internal/**, or does it fall through to anyRequest().authenticated()?

Even if the InternalServiceTokenFilter's path check is bypassed, is there a second, independent authorization layer (OnBehalfAuthResolver) guarding the specific routes named (messages, turns/release)?
Can a normal logged-in user ever obtain a validly-signed on-behalf JWT, or is it purely server-to-server and never exposed to the browser?
In CampaignService.create(), is CampaignStatus client-controllable, or is it forced to DRAFT server-side?
Are requireFundedEscrow() and chargeOnPublish() invoked anywhere inside create(), or only inside update()'s transitioningToActive branch?
Does validateStatusForWorkspace() (called from create()) enforce anything beyond workspace verification status (i.e. does it check escrow or fees)?
Is there an existing test that exercises create() with status=ACTIVE, or do all activation-gate tests only cover the PATCH path?
Are influora-ai/env.example and influora-api/env.example actually tracked by git (not gitignored), and present across multiple historical commits?
Do the committed key values match live-provider key formats (length/prefix) rather than obvious placeholders like 'your-key-here'?
Does a code comment in env.example claim 'no real secrets' in a way that contradicts the actual committed values (a known repo pattern of misleading comments)?
Is there independent evidence the keys are currently active/valid, or does that remain unverified (limiting evidence to committed-format only, not live-key confirmation)?

verdicts.reason: Independently opened all three cited files at the RC. InternalServiceTokenFilter.java:82-83 confirmed: `String path = stripContext(request.getRequestURI())` then `if (!path.startsWith(INTERNAL_PREFIX))` — getRequestURI() is the raw, percent-still-encoded URI per servlet spec, so a request to e.g. /api/v1/%69nternal/meera/turns/release would not match this literal prefix check and the filter would no-op via chain.doFilter, skipping the JWT+HMAC dual-credential check entirely. SecurityConfig.java confirmed at line 298: the authorization chain ends in `.anyRequest().authenticated()` with no explicit requestMatchers entry for /internal/** (unlike /admin/** and /creator/**, which do have explicit hasRole rules) — so once the filter is bypassed, Spring Security's own gate is satisfied by ANY authenticated user (BRAND/CREATOR/ADMIN), not just the mesh service. MeeraInternalController.java:319-372 confirmed to contain exactly the two routes claimed: POST /messages (persistTurnWriteback, forges assistant turn content) and POST /turns/release (releaseTurnCredit, refunds AI credit for a turn). No spring.mvc.pathmatch override or custom HttpFirewall/UrlPathHelper was found in the RC (grepped config + resources), so Spring Boot 3.3.5's default PathPatternParser-based MVC routing (which matches on the decoded path) would very likely still dispatch a %69nternal request to the real controller even though the raw-URI filter waved it through — this is the classic decoded-vs-raw path confusion class of bug. IMPORTANT REFINEMENT the original finder did not cite: both target routes still sit behind a SECOND, independent gate — OnBehalfAuthResolver.resolveForWorkspace — which requires a correctly-signed on-behalf JWT whose workspaceId/conversationId claims match the request. This is not bypassed by the percent-encoding trick (it runs in the controller/service, not in URI-prefix matching), so the attack is not a bare auth-bypass into an arbitrary victim's data. However, I found corroborating evidence that makes the attack concretely exploitable rather than merely theoretical: MeeraSessionService.java lines 439-443 show the on-behalf token is minted and returned directly in the TurnResult sent to the browser, with an explicit comment 'the browser forwards THIS as onbehalf_jwt' — i.e. every normal Meera user already legitimately receives a validly-signed on-behalf JWT for their own workspace/conversation as part of ordinary chat use. Combined with the filter-bypass, a logged-in brand/creator user can extract their own legitimately-issued on-behalf JWT from a normal chat turn and then call /internal/meera/turns/release directly to fraudulently reclaim an AI-credit refund on a turn that did not genuinely fail (defeating the documented invariant that this route exists ONLY for genuine provider failures — see the 'SECURITY FIX (Wave 2 round 2, Kabir FAILs #1/#2)' javadoc on releaseTurnCredit, meaning this exact class of abuse was already flagged once before), and/or call /messages to inject fabricated assistant content into their own conversation history. Scope correction: exploitation is confined to the attacker's OWN workspace/conversation (the on-behalf token is workspace/conversation-bound), not arbitrary victims — the finding's title does not explicitly claim cross-tenant impact, so this is not a refutation, but it does mean the blast radius is 'financial/self-serving fraud at scale across many accounts' rather than 'account takeover of others.' Did not execute a live runtime reproduction (would require standing up the full Spring Boot stack + Python mesh service + valid signing secrets), so evidence stays at code+config analysis (E3) rather than E4/CONFIRMED-RUNTIME. Provenance COMMITTED, confirmed present at 115f698 with no local modifications.
verdicts.new_evidence: MeeraSessionService.java:439-443 — onBehalfToken is minted and returned to the browser in TurnResult ('the browser forwards THIS as onbehalf_jwt'), meaning a normal user can legitimately harvest a validly-signed on-behalf JWT for their own workspace during ordinary use, which is what turns the raw-URI filter's path-matching flaw into a concretely reachable exploit against turns/release and /messages rather than a purely theoretical filter gap.

verdicts.reason: Read CampaignService.java lines 145-235 (create()) in full at the RC. CampaignWriteRequest.status (CampaignDtos.java ~line 63) is a plain client-supplied field with no bean-validation restriction to DRAFT; create() does `CampaignStatus status = req.status() != null ? req.status() : CampaignStatus.DRAFT` (line 170) and then only calls `validator.validateStatusForWorkspace(status, workspace)` (line 171). Opened CampaignValidator.java:62-70 — validateStatusForWorkspace only checks `workspace.getVerificationStatus() == VERIFIED` before allowing ACTIVE; it contains no escrow or fee logic whatsoever. Read the rest of create() (through line 235, the campaignRepository.save/return) and confirmed there is no call to requireFundedEscrow(...) or brandCampaignFeeService.chargeOnPublish(...) anywhere in the method. Those two calls exist ONLY inside update() at lines 368-377, gated on `transitioningToActive` (a DRAFT/PAUSED/PENDING_APPROVAL -> ACTIVE patch transition) — confirmed by reading update() end-to-end. Role gating on create() (OWNER/ADMIN/MANAGER, line 152) does not substitute for an escrow/fee check — a legitimate MANAGER-level user in a VERIFIED workspace can POST /campaigns with `status: 'ACTIVE'` in the body and the campaign is persisted directly as ACTIVE with zero EscrowHold rows and zero publish-fee charge, exactly as claimed. Also checked CampaignActivationGatesTest.java: its three test methods (testHumanPatchToActiveRejectedWithoutFundedEscrow, ...WithOnlyPendingEscrow, ...SucceedsWithFundedEscrow) all target the PATCH/update() path only — there is no test in the RC that exercises create() with status=ACTIVE, confirming this is an untested gap, not merely an untested-but-covered-elsewhere scenario. Did not execute a runtime test since RC source is read-only for this audit and a new Spring context test would take more setup than the effort budget allows; the code path itself is short, unambiguous, and leaves no room for a hidden guard (no AOP/aspect, no @PrePersist hook, no DB trigger found referencing escrow on the campaigns table). This matches the disagreement note that an uncommitted F-0848 rewrite may close the gap, but is not part of this RC — confirms provenance COMMITTED and PRESENT in the RC exactly as claimed.
verdicts.new_evidence: Confirmed no CampaignActivationGatesTest (or any other test in the RC) exercises the create()-to-ACTIVE path; all existing coverage is PATCH-only, so the gap has zero regression protection in the committed test suite.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed both files are git-tracked at the RC via `git ls-files` (influora-ai/env.example, influora-api/env.example) and present across 7 historical commits each (`git log --follow`), so this is genuinely baked into git history, not a one-off working-tree artifact. Inspected the cited lines with values redacted after 6-8 characters (never printed in full, per audit safety rules) and computed length/format heuristics without exposing secret bytes: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is 108 chars starting 'sk-ant-a' (matches Anthropic's real key format/length, not a placeholder); GEMINI_API_KEY is 35 chars starting 'AIzaSy-' (matches Google API key format); SARVAM_API_KEY is 36 chars starting 'sk_77nef...'; R2_ACCOUNT_ID is exactly 32 hex chars, R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID exactly 32 hex chars, and R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY exactly 64 hex chars — all matching Cloudflare R2's real identifier/key lengths (a hand-written placeholder would essentially never coincidentally hit these exact hex lengths); MSG91_AUTH_KEY/MSG91_TOKEN_AUTH are 27-char alphanumeric tokens with no placeholder markers. None of the inspected values contain placeholder markers ('your', 'xxx', 'changeme', 'replace', 'example', angle brackets, asterisks). Notably, influora-ai/env.example carries an explicit header comment claiming 'NO REAL SECRETS COMMITTED HERE... this service holds ONLY the values below' directly above a live-format ANTHROPIC_API_KEY/GEMINI_API_KEY/SARVAM_API_KEY block — a comment that is directly contradicted by the file's own content, consistent with this repo's documented pattern of stale/misleading comments (per team memory on stale-comment audits). Downgraded evidence_score from the finder's original 4 to 3: format/length/entropy analysis is strong static (code+config) evidence that these are live-shaped credentials, but I did NOT attempt to call any provider API to confirm the keys are currently active (this would be an unauthorized live action against a third-party's account and is explicitly out of scope/unsafe for this audit), so 'still active' genuinely remains unverified — matching the original finder's own disagreement note. Regardless of current activity, committed live-format secrets in tracked files across multiple historical commits independently justify P0 (rotation + git-history purge required as a precaution) even if some/all happen to have since been rotated by the team outside this repo.
verdicts.new_evidence: influora-ai/env.example's own header comment ('NO REAL SECRETS COMMITTED HERE') directly contradicts the live-format key values that follow it in the same file — an internal inconsistency that strengthens rather than weakens the finding.
